title: Small Children, Big Ideas
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Mary Myatt reports a conversation with Vicky Paul, a Year 1 teacher and curriculum lead, about using rich picture books to deepen existing geography teaching. In a sequence comparing Edinburgh and Addis Ababa, pupils handled artefacts such as tartan and tablet, and those with pencil-control difficulties built a 3D map of Edinburgh landmarks from wooden blocks while using precise geographical language. Another sequence used a book that unfolds into a globe, and a pupil with significant speech and language needs contributed fully through symbols and sentence stems. Myatt highlights the school's use of digital floor books to evidence understanding rather than task completion, the pride pupils take in work that has dignity, and a headteacher who funded books and gave staff time to choose them. The takeaway is that inclusion means changing the means of access while keeping the content ambitious.
points: Starting with a book and existing geography planning, not a new unit, made the change manageable for a busy teacher.
Artefacts, wooden-block maps and symbols changed how pupils accessed the content without lowering the ambition of the subject.
Completing an activity is not the same as understanding the curriculum, so digital floor books capture dialogue and photographs to test whether children can explain their learning later.
When the final outcome has dignity, pupils take extraordinary care over handwriting and presentation.
Whole-school change needs leadership support in funding, professional freedom and time for staff to browse and choose books.
quotes: Her starting point was refreshingly straightforward: take a book, consider what it offers, and try something worthwhile with existing geography planning rather than inventing an entire unit from scratch.
The subject content remained uncompromisingly ambitious. What shifted was the means of access, captured through photographs and verbatim dialogue rather than completing a worksheet.
Participation means having something genuine to contribute that is recognised as worthwhile by the community of the classroom.
A copied sentence or coloured-in sheet shows task completion, but it tells us very little about what a child understands.
Saying “we made a map” describes an activity; explaining the features of that map begins to show geographical thinking.
True inclusion is never about watering down the curriculum. Vicky’s work points to a much better question: what might this subject make possible for this child?
